distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer disease leaf for infection and inflammation of the female upper genital tract. Gonococcal, chlamydial, polymicrobial, anaerobic, IUD-associated, postpartum, post-procedure, tubo-ovarian abscess, perihepatitis, severe, septic, recurrent, and chronic-sequela contexts remain axes, modifiers, event hazards, source-control states, or future subtype layers rather than disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation ranking may consume lower abdominal or pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness, uterine or adnexal tenderness, discharge, fever, systemic inflammatory labs, and initial pelvic imaging. NAAT or culture pathogen identity, laparoscopy, operative findings, pathology, final paper diagnosis, treatment response, and follow-up outcomes remain confirmatory or non-ranking unless a post-workup mode explicitly consumes them.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Lower genital tract pathogen burden or dysbiosis
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Cervicovaginal Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, bacterial-vaginosis-associated anaerobes, enteric organisms, respiratory flora, or mixed vaginal flora create the microbial substrate for upper-tract ascent.
Microbes ascend through the endocervix into endometrium and tubes, favored by mucosal disruption, menses, postpartum or post-procedure state, IUD context, or untreated cervicitis.
Neutrophilic upper-genital-tract inflammation involves endometrium, fallopian tubes, ovaries, or adjacent pelvic tissues and produces cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness.

Anaerobes and mixed aerobic organisms sustain severe salpingitis, endometritis, pelvic peritonitis, and abscess formation; pathogen identity is a treatment context rather than part of the first-layer leaf name.

Inflamed tubes, ovaries, endometrium, and purulent exudate irritate pelvic peritoneum and adjacent bowel or bladder, producing lower abdominal pain, tenderness, guarding, urinary symptoms, or reactive bowel findings.
Upper-genital-tract infection and pelvic inflammation can drive fever, chills, tachycardia, leukocytosis, neutrophilia, CRP/PCT rise, and in severe cases sepsis physiology.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Tubo-ovarian inflammatory mass or abscess formation
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Persistent salpingitis and oophoritis can organize into phlegmon, pyosalpinx, hydrosalpinx, or a complex tubo-ovarian abscess involving tube, ovary, and surrounding pelvic organs.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Abscess rupture, diffuse peritonitis, or source-control failure
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Large, ruptured, poorly penetrated, or undrained pelvic collections can spill pus into peritoneal or extraperitoneal spaces, sustain burden despite antibiotics, and drive shock or organ-risk cascades.
Inflammation can track along peritoneal surfaces to the hepatic capsule, causing Fitz-Hugh-Curtis physiology with right upper quadrant pleuritic or movement-related pain and capsular enhancement.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Tubal epithelial injury, adhesions, and reproductive sequelae
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Inflammation damages cilia, epithelium, tubal patency, and pelvic surfaces, creating chronic pelvic pain, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, hydrosalpinx, and recurrent PID risk.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Active antimicrobial coverage and source-control resolution
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Concordant broad-spectrum coverage, anaerobic coverage, oral absorption or IV exposure, drainage or surgery when needed, and partner/source management reshape the trajectory toward microbial clearance and resolving inflammation.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Lower-tract organisms or dysbiosis create the microbial substrate that can ascend into the upper genital tract.
Ascending infection produces endometritis, salpingitis, oophoritis, and adjacent pelvic inflammation.
BV-associated flora and mixed organisms often participate in PID and complicated abscess phenotypes.
Anaerobic and mixed flora sustain upper-tract inflammatory burden.
Inflamed tubes, ovaries, and endometrium irritate pelvic peritoneum and adjacent organs.
Upper-tract infection produces systemic cytokine and leukocyte responses.
Persistent salpingitis and oophoritis can organize into pyosalpinx, phlegmon, or tubo-ovarian abscess.
Anaerobic and mixed flora are prominent in abscess formation and persistence.
Large or uncontrolled tubo-ovarian abscess can rupture, spread, or persist without drainage/source control.
Peritoneal inflammatory spread can involve the hepatic capsule.
Inflammation damages tubal epithelium and pelvic surfaces over days to weeks.
Active antimicrobial therapy reduces lower-tract and ascending microbial burden.
Concordant therapy allows upper-genital-tract inflammation to resolve.
Drainage or operation plus active antibiotics reduces uncontrolled abscess/source activity.
Cervicitis or endocervical inflammation can produce mucopurulent discharge.
PID often coexists with abnormal cervical or vaginal discharge, though discharge can be absent.
Movement of the cervix transmits traction to inflamed upper genital structures.
Endometritis and myometrial/peritoneal irritation can produce uterine tenderness.
Salpingitis, oophoritis, pyosalpinx, or TOA produce adnexal tenderness.
Pelvic peritoneal inflammation is the main driver of pelvic pain.
PID commonly presents with bilateral or poorly localized lower abdominal pain.
Bladder-adjacent pelvic inflammation can create suprapubic pain or pressure.
Pelvic inflammation produces lower abdominal tenderness.
Severe pelvic peritonitis or rupture can cause guarding or rebound.
Adjacent bladder irritation or concurrent urethritis/cervicitis can produce dysuria, while sterile urinalysis may remain present.
Pelvic organ and peritoneal inflammation can worsen pain with intercourse.
Systemic inflammation can raise measured temperature, although afebrile PID is common.
Subjective or measured fever can accompany upper-tract infection and TOA.
Fever, pain, inflammation, dehydration, or shock raises heart rate.
Leukocytosis is common in acute PID and especially TOA.
Bacterial upper-tract inflammation often causes neutrophil predominance.
CRP rises with inflammatory and abscess burden.
Procalcitonin can rise in severe bacterial PID or ruptured TOA with sepsis physiology.
TOA is the observed complex inflammatory adnexal mass or abscess state.
Abscess formation increases measurable complex adnexal mass size.
TOA, pyosalpinx, hydrosalpinx, and phlegmon can appear as a complex adnexal mass.
Inflammatory extension around adnexa produces fat stranding on CT or MRI.
A complex pelvic collection can become a drainable source-control target.
Large abscess, rupture, nonresponse, or sepsis increases source-control need.
Rupture or severe exudative inflammation produces pelvic free fluid.
Uncontrolled or large TOA raises rupture risk.
Pus spillage produces diffuse pelvic or generalized peritonitis.
Rupture, source-control failure, and high burden can progress to septic shock.
Hepatic capsular inflammation causes RUQ pain in Fitz-Hugh-Curtis physiology.
Perihepatitis can enhance along the hepatic capsule on dynamic contrast imaging.
Adhesions and chronic inflammation raise chronic pelvic pain risk.
Tubal scarring and occlusion increase infertility risk.
Damaged tubal ciliary transport and scarring increase ectopic pregnancy risk.
Septic shock is the main short-term mortality pathway in severe PID or ruptured TOA.
Diffuse peritonitis raises mortality through sepsis, organ dysfunction, and operative risk.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: CMT and adnexal tenderness commonly co-occur from upper-genital-tract inflammation but can be incomplete.
Bimanual tenderness axes are related exam outputs, not hard diagnostic labels.
Cervical discharge often contributes to abnormal vaginal discharge, but either may be absent or nonspecific.
WBC and CRP often rise together with inflammatory burden, though timing and host factors vary.
A larger measured complex adnexal collection should imply a present TOA activity parent.
TOA increases drainage or surgical-source-control pressure, especially when large, ruptured, septic, or nonresponsive.
Rupture or pus spillage produces peritoneal irritation and generalized infection risk.
Diffuse peritonitis increases septic shock hazard.
Shock dominates near-term death risk in PID.
Tubal and pelvic adhesions raise chronic pain risk without making chronic pain a separate disease leaf here.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: The bundle helps only when it covers the true pathogen mix.
Vomiting, severe illness, or poor adherence makes oral doxycycline/metronidazole unreliable.
TOA may require IV therapy, observation, and drainage assessment.
Pregnancy changes disposition and antimicrobial safety context.

failure_modes: M genitalium or resistant pathogen context

side_effects.interpretation: Doxycycline and metronidazole can cause GI intolerance.

treatments.context_specific_role: Broad empiric coverage vector for mild to moderate presentations when oral completion and follow-up are reliable.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: TOA or severe illness increases value of parenteral monitored therapy.
Antibiotics alone may not control a large, ruptured, or inaccessible abscess.
Anaerobic coverage is important in PID and TOA.

side_effects.interpretation: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea or metronidazole intolerance can occur.

treatments.context_specific_role: Parenteral active-coverage vector for TOA, inability to tolerate oral therapy, severe illness, pregnancy context, or failed outpatient trajectory.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cefoxitin/cefotetan provide stronger anaerobic coverage than some other cephalosporin paths.
Severe beta-lactam allergy constrains cephalosporin use.

treatments.context_specific_role: Cephalosporin-based PID coverage lane when local regimen design and allergy context fit.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: This lane covers many mixed aerobic/anaerobic TOA contexts.
Renal impairment changes exposure and toxicity rather than disease identity.

side_effects.interpretation: Broad-spectrum beta-lactam exposure can cause diarrhea.

treatments.context_specific_role: Mixed-flora parenteral lane, especially when TOA or anaerobic context is prominent and allergy context permits.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Gentamicin toxicity and dosing become limiting with kidney vulnerability.
Clindamycin provides anaerobic coverage useful in TOA context.

side_effects.interpretation: Aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity risk depends on exposure and baseline kidney function.

treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative parenteral lane when cephalosporin paths are unsuitable or local care path favors clindamycin/gentamicin.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Persistent PID symptoms or documented M genitalium context can change the active-coverage path.
Fluoroquinolone safety is constrained in pregnancy.

failure_modes: using this lane without broad PID coverage when mixed infection remains plausible

side_effects.interpretation: Fluoroquinolone QT risk in susceptible contexts.

treatments.context_specific_role: Coverage-adjustment lane for documented or strongly suspected M genitalium/persistent PID context.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Drainage helps only when a collection can be accessed.
Small uncomplicated PID without drainable abscess does not benefit from drainage.
Drainage without active therapy may not clear mixed pelvic infection.

side_effects.interpretation: Drainage procedure bleeding risk depends on access route and coagulopathy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Source-control vector for drainable TOA or pelvic abscess, particularly with large collection, nonresponse, rupture risk, or sepsis physiology.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Diffuse peritonitis increases value of urgent operative control.
Shock from ruptured abscess requires rapid source control plus resuscitation.
Operation only helps if pus and infected tissue are adequately controlled.

failure_modes: operative injury in distorted pelvic anatomy

side_effects.interpretation: Operative blood loss and dilution can lower hemoglobin.

treatments.context_specific_role: Operative vector for ruptured TOA, diffuse peritonitis, failed drainage, bowel involvement, diagnostic uncertainty with surgical emergency, or life-threatening sepsis.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Shock physiology increases benefit of fluids, vasopressors, monitoring, and ICU support.
Resuscitation supports physiology but does not sterilize or drain the source.

side_effects.interpretation: Over-resuscitation can worsen oxygenation in susceptible hosts.

treatments.context_specific_role: Physiologic support for hypotension, tachycardia, AKI risk, or shock while antimicrobial and source-control vectors address the cause.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Symptom improvement alone should not be interpreted as abscess control.

side_effects.interpretation: Opioid-heavy analgesia can worsen constipation or ileus-like symptoms.

treatments.context_specific_role: Supportive symptom vector with serial exam and 48-72 hour reassessment; not a replacement for active coverage.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Recent unprotected exposure or STI-positive partner raises PID prior probability.
Chlamydia exposure changes pathogen coverage context.
Gonorrhea remains a key PID pathogen even when testing is pending.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises prior probability and shifts treatment context toward STI-active coverage while allowing negative NAAT to remain non-exclusionary.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Young age and partner change are epidemiologic risk contexts.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises prior probability without narrowing the first-layer PID phenotype.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: BV-associated anaerobes participate in PID and tubal epithelial injury.
Anaerobic context increases value of anaerobic coverage.

present.trajectory_modulation: Shifts toward polymicrobial/anaerobic burden and sequela risk.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: IUD context is a local risk and source context for selected PID/actinomycotic-like infections.
Long-duration retained devices can be associated with chronic pelvic inflammatory masses.
Device removal or source review can be relevant.

present.trajectory_modulation: Adds device-source context without making IUD-associated PID a separate first-layer disease name.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Recent delivery, abortion, or uterine procedure changes ascent and pathogen-source context.
Mucosal disruption can facilitate upper-tract spread.
Postpartum or procedural pelvic infection can be polymicrobial and anaerobic.

present.trajectory_modulation: Shifts source and organism context while remaining within the PID spectrum.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Prior inflammation increases adhesions, pain, infertility, and recurrence context.
Prior damage raises chronic pain risk.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises recurrence and sequelae without using previous diagnosis as a hard label.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Large or persistent abscess increases drainage or surgery pressure.
Large abscess and nonresponse raise rupture risk.
Complicated abscess phenotypes increase near-term risk.
Pregnancy is a treatment-safety and disposition context.
Maternal morbidity and obstetric risk lower tolerance for outpatient or unsafe treatment paths.

present.trajectory_modulation: Pregnancy changes treatment and monitoring context rather than defining the PID leaf.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Fever can be absent despite severe infection.
Lower host reserve raises severe infection hazard.
Comorbidity increases kidney vulnerability during sepsis or nephrotoxic therapy.

present.trajectory_modulation: Can blunt classic inflammatory signs while increasing complication and treatment-toxicity risk.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Delay or inactive therapy permits abscess persistence or enlargement.
Missed source control sustains burden and rupture/shock hazard.
Uncontrolled source and delayed active therapy worsen severe PID outcomes.

present.trajectory_modulation: Prolongs disease until active coverage and source control are achieved.

supportive_care: Structure pelvic exam evidence directly: cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, adnexal tenderness, discharge, pelvic mass, and peritoneal signs should be observed axes rather than a hidden diagnosis label.
Do not use negative cervical/vaginal gonorrhea or chlamydia NAAT to exclude PID in presentation-only ranking; upper-tract infection can persist when lower-tract testing is negative.

Test for pregnancy, gonorrhea, chlamydia, HIV, syphilis, trichomonas/BV context, and other STI or pregnancy contexts because they reshape treatment, safety, and partner management rather than the PID disease name.

Use pelvic ultrasound, CT, or MRI findings when available: salpingitis, hydrosalpinx, pyosalpinx, complex adnexal mass, TOA size, pelvic free fluid, fat stranding, and perihepatitis should be mapped as axes.

Keep operative findings, laparoscopy, histopathology, abscess culture species, susceptibility, and response to antibiotics or drainage in confirmatory or post-workup fields for presentation-only tests.

Reassess within 48-72 hours after outpatient therapy; worsening pain, fever, vomiting, leukocytosis, TOA, pregnancy, or inability to tolerate oral therapy should move the state toward parenteral therapy and source-control assessment.

Evaluate appendicitis, diverticulitis, pyelonephritis, ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, endometriosis, malignancy, inflammatory bowel disease, urinary infection, and sepsis leaves fairly when their observed axes are present.

Source control is a state variable: drainable TOA, rupture, diffuse peritonitis, failed medical therapy, extraperitoneal extension, bowel involvement, and distorted pelvic anatomy determine whether drainage or operation changes RMST.

Partner notification, abstinence until treatment completion and symptom resolution, and treatment of recent partners affect reinfection and public health context but should not be encoded as first-line labels.
quality_notes: Tubo-ovarian abscess, postpartum context, IUD context, pathogen identity, rupture, and septic physiology are axes or modifiers inside the first-layer PID spectrum, not disease-name qualifiers.

New pelvic exam and adnexal imaging axes are reusable ontology candidates for gynecologic infection and should be reviewed horizontally when related leaves such as tubo-ovarian abscess or postpartum endometritis are added.
